To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the high genetic diversity of E. coli and K. pneumoniae carrying clinically relevant ESBL and AmpC genes, including emerging IncI1/ ST12 plasmids, was revealed in corvids across Canada.

1) E. coli isolations from corvids in Canada are genetically diverse and include clinically important clones and plasmids; 2) E. coli carrying AmpC beta-lacatmase and extended-spectrum betalactamase genes are widespread throughout Canada and are likely a threat to public health.

(a) Canadian wildlife are colonized with E. coli and K. pneumoniae isolates carrying AmpC and ESβL genes, including clinically relevant clones and emerging plamids; (b) AmpC and ES β-lactamase genes were predominantly carried on plasmids belonging to incompatibility groups IncI1 (ST12) and IncA/C, respectively; and (c) blaCTX-M-15 was not detected.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular characterization of plasmids and the genetic relatedness of faecal bacteria of corvids.
the detection, characterization and spread of antibiotic resistance genes in wildlife.
the molecular epidemiology of ESBL- and AmpC-producing bacteria among Canadian wild birds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the study indicate that the Canadian corvids are a source of ESBL/AmpC producing bacteria.
the presence of AmpC beta-lactalmas and extended-spectrum cephalosporin resistance in corvids is of concern and may be an important reservoir of these resistance genes.
corvids are a source of plasmids carrying clinically important AmpC and ES BL genes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

corvids are a potential reservoir of plasmids and genes for resistance to antimicrobials in Canada, and that these birds could serve as a reservoir for the dissemination of resistance genes to humans.
the Canadian corvids were found to carry diverse AmpC and ES BL genes and plasmids.
the Canadian corvids are a reservoir of plasmids that carry blaCMY-1 and blaCMY2 genes and blaCTX-M genes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
corvids can be reservoirs of clinically important ESBL and AmpC beta-lacatmase genes.

we identified several plasmids that are associated with the dissemination of AmpC beta-lacatmase- and ESBL-producing E. coli and K. pneumoniae in corvids, and these plasmids have been previously reported in humans.
the corvids in Canada are a reservoir of ESBL and AmpC genes and associated plamids.
